parts.name: Bradawl
parts.desc: A hardened point no wider than a pin, ground for the longest spin in the game and almost no travel at all.
parts.rationale: Sibling: needle. stamina 1.66 is 24 percent past the Tier 1 top of 1.34; drive 0.32 is 36 percent below the Tier 1 floor of 0.50, so the pay is further than the push. Everything else is at or under needle (stable 0.92 vs 1.05, shaft 1.02 vs 1.10) so it is not strictly better than its sibling on any axis but stamina. Physical story: a contact patch that small has almost no friction to lose spin to and almost nothing to push the top around the dish. Measured ceiling 57.5, pull 47.3 against needle 53.2, point 44.5, taper 43.6.

parts.name: Still Pin
parts.desc: It parks where you launch it and stays there; the smallest solid hit puts it on its side.
parts.rationale: Sibling: point. The push is drive taken 28 percent BELOW the Tier 1 floor, because low drive is the benefit here: it drops the equilibrium lean and the travel term in spin decay, which is exactly the boss Post identity as a player part. stable 0.56 is 32 percent below the floor of 0.82, a bigger move than the push. It is worse than point on stamina, stable, dash and shaft, so the only thing it wins is standing still. Physical story: a tip ground dead vertical with no rake gives no sideways push and no righting moment either. Measured ceiling 41.3, pull 40.2.

parts.name: Spur
parts.desc: The foot is ground on a slant so friction turns into travel, and every jolt it earns goes straight up the thin shank into the teeth.
parts.rationale: Sibling: claw. drive 2.15 is only 14 percent past claw's 1.88 on paper, and that is deliberate: the simulation charges the rest of the push itself. The slip term in spin decay is proportional to the drive FORCE, which is proportional to drive times lean, and lean at equilibrium is itself proportional to drive, so spin cost scales roughly as drive squared. I measured the cliff on the attack chassis: ceiling 61.3 at drive 2.10, 36.3 at 2.35, where a 2.35 tip loses 300 of 400 rounds to its own spinout. So 2.15 IS the 25 percent push once the physics bill is paid. shaft 0.56 is 28 percent below the floor. Identical to claw on stamina, stable and mass, better only on drive, worse on dash and shaft. Measured ceiling 56.3, pull 12.3, the lowest pull in the slot and well clear of the creep gate; if you want it nearer claw's 25 the honest dial is shaft 0.56 to 0.68, worth roughly 6 points.

parts.name: Rowel
parts.desc: A toothed wheel of a tip that hooks the rail harder than anything stock, on a contact ring too small to right itself.
parts.rationale: Sibling: gearf. dash 2.32 is 25 percent past gearf's 1.85; stable 0.48 is 41 percent below the floor of 0.82, comfortably further than the push. Note the push is partly self limiting by design: rail grip saturates at dash 1.85, so everything above that buys only dash gain and easier engagement while dashCost scales linearly, 20.9 spin per dash against gearf's 16.7. Worse than gearf on drive, stable and shaft, equal on stamina and mass. Physical story: a deep toothed ring grips the rail and stands the top on a knife edge of contact. Measured ceiling 58.8, pull 27.6 against flat 27.9 and gearf 36.0. An earlier version at stable 0.56 read pull 33.5 and tripped the creep gate, so stable is the dial to watch here.

parts.name: Sabot
parts.desc: A broad wooden shoe of a foot that nothing tips over, seated in a soft collar that hands every shock to the lock teeth.
parts.rationale: Sibling: dome. MIDDLE PROFILE, one of the three the brief asked for: stamina 1.00, drive 0.88 and dash 0.60 all sit mid range, so a mixed build can fit it without rebuilding around it. stable 1.55 is 25 percent past dome's 1.24; shaft 0.55 is 29 percent below the floor. Worse than dome on stamina, drive, dash and shaft, better only on stable. Physical story: a wide soft pad has a huge righting moment and no stiffness, so the shock that does not tip the top goes up the shaft instead. It is the deliberate mirror of Ferrule. Measured ceiling 65.0, pull 49.6 against dome 56.2 and ball 48.1.

parts.name: Ferrule
parts.desc: A long steel collar driven deep into the shaft so no impact reaches the teeth, standing on a foot too narrow to hold you up.
parts.rationale: Sibling: spool. MIDDLE PROFILE: stamina 1.06, drive 1.00, dash 0.72. shaft 1.48 is 25 percent past spool's slot maximum of 1.18; stable 0.60 is 27 percent below the floor. Strictly worse than spool on stamina, drive, stable and dash, better only on shaft, which is the whole trade. Physical story: to get the shank that deep you give up the flare at the bottom, so the burst resistance is bought with the contact patch. Mirror of Sabot: one buys standing up with fragility, the other buys staying together with falling over. Measured ceiling 46.3, pull 39.9 against spool 46.6.

parts.name: Cleat
parts.desc: A knurled stud that takes the rail on an ordinary top, bought with a shank that pops apart under one solid blow.
parts.rationale: Sibling: spool. MIDDLE PROFILE and the most important part in this proposal: it is the answer to the note that the rail dash currently only exists inside a coherent attack chassis. dash 2.26 is 22 percent past 1.85 while stamina and drive both sit at 1.02, so a stamina or defense build can buy the rail route without becoming an attack top. shaft 0.54 is 31 percent below the floor, further than the push, and it is a savage cost: on the common 3-60 ratchet burstResist falls to 0.43 and incoming wear roughly doubles. Worse than spool on stamina, drive, stable and shaft. Measured ceiling 41.3, pull 34.8 against spool 46.6, so it is a real option and not a free upgrade.

parts.name: Plumb
parts.desc: All the metal is in the foot, so shoves barely move it and the loaded tip grinds its spin into the floor.
parts.rationale: Sibling: ball. mass 0.0064 is 28 percent past the slot maximum of 0.0050; stamina 0.54 is 31 percent below the floor, further than the push. Mass is the honest push here because in this simulation the incoming normal impulse and the shock spin drain are both divided by the top's mass, so metal buys immovability; and rule three says mass at the centre just loads the tip, which is exactly what the stamina bill pays for. drive 0.68 also puts it under the Deadweight rig threshold of 0.7, so it is the bit that turns that rig on. Worse than ball on stamina, drive, dash and shaft. Measured ceiling 52.5, pull 49.2 against ball 48.1 and dome 56.2. Watch this one on the full audit: an earlier version with stable 1.18 and shaft 1.16 read ceiling 72.9 and was the second strongest bit in the slot, so the trimmed stable and shaft are load bearing.

parts.name: Agate
parts.desc: A polished stone pivot with almost no friction at all, which also means almost nothing to stand it back up.
parts.rationale: Sibling: taper. stamina 1.72 is 28 percent past 1.34; stable 0.54 is 34 percent below the floor, further than the push. This is the deliberate counterpart to Bradawl: same push, different currency. Bradawl keeps its footing and gives up all travel, Agate keeps a little travel and gives up its righting moment, so it dies by toppling at high spin rather than by running out. Worse than taper on drive, stable, dash and shaft. Physical story: agate is the real material for a low friction pivot bearing and a mirror polished stone gives the tip friction nothing to work with in either direction. Measured ceiling 42.5, pull 39.2 against taper 43.6.

parts.name: Corundum
parts.desc: A jewelled pivot that runs longer than anything else and charges in a hurry, and it will never coast to a win.
parts.rationale: Sibling: needle. stamina 1.95 is 46 percent past the Tier 1 top, the longest running tip in the game; drive 0.30 is 40 percent below the floor. Greedy is the sharpest possible anti synergy and that is the point: the tip whose only route is outlasting you is the one that cannot win by outlasting you. Measured on the four reference chassis, greedy converts its 1 point spinout losses into 2 point knockouts, 62 becoming 156 in 1200 rounds, while spinout losses fall 306 to 205. IMPORTANT for the audit: that cost lands on the SCOREBOARD, not on round win rate, which moved only +0.5, so partaudit's pull metric cannot see it. It passes anyway on pull, 41.2 against needle 53.2 and point 44.5, but a points weighted audit would show the real bill. Measured ceiling 50.0.

parts.name: Rasp
parts.desc: Coarse cut teeth that bite the rail like nothing in the catalogue, on a top that slides out of the dish at speeds anything else survives.
parts.rationale: Sibling: gearf, and the Relic extension of Rowel. dash 2.75 is 49 percent past 1.85; stable 0.46 is 44 percent below the floor. The push pays for itself twice over inside the physics: dashCost is 24.8 spin per dash against gearf's 16.7, up to three dashes a second on the rail. Skittish is the new drawback and it fires exactly where it should, on the rail: measured on the reference chassis it doubles ringout losses, 127 to 266 in 1200 rounds, and costs 2.0 points of win rate plus 2 points of score every time it fires. Measured ceiling 58.8, pull 27.6 against claw 25.2 and flat 27.9, so it sits just inside the gate; stable is the dial if the full audit disagrees.

parts.name: Cobble
parts.desc: A wide flat stone of a foot that will not be tipped over, sitting so loose in the seat that one connected blow pops it apart.
parts.rationale: Sibling: dome. stable 1.72 is 39 percent past 1.24 and Loose Lock multiplies it again by 1.3 inside build, giving an effective 2.24 and a stability threshold near 218 rad per second against a stock 340, so it stands up almost to a standstill. shaft 0.54 is 31 percent below the floor and Loose Lock halves burstResist on top of it, so on a 5-60 ratchet the lock is 0.27 and incoming wear runs nearly four times normal. Measured on the reference chassis the drawback costs 13.0 points of win rate and doubles burst losses, 259 to 500 in 1200 rounds. That is the whole part: it cannot be knocked over and it can be opened in one blow, which teaches burst as the answer to the immovable. Measured ceiling 63.7, pull 37.6 against dome 56.2 and ball 48.1.

parts.name: Pintle
parts.desc: The shank goes the full depth of the shaft so nothing bursts it, ending in a polished dome with nothing to keep it inside the lip.
parts.rationale: Sibling: ball. shaft 1.72 is 46 percent past the slot maximum of 1.18; paired with a 9-60 ratchet burstResist reaches 2.20 and it is effectively unburstable. drive 0.30 is 40 percent below the floor, so it cannot chase anything. Skittish is the drawback that actually bites this profile: measured on the four reference chassis it costs 6.2 points of win rate and lifts ringout losses from 161 to 278 in 1200 rounds, which is the right shape, because a top you cannot burst and cannot topple has to be steered out instead. I first wrote a decay based drawback for it and measured the effect at 0.3 points, effectively zero, because a defensive top on these chassis survives the full 60 second limit on spin alone; that version is dropped, see notes. Measured ceiling 55.0, pull 44.1 against ball 48.1.

parts.name: Jasper
parts.desc: So slick it barely travels at all, and brittle enough that once it is tired every hit lands twice as hard.
parts.rationale: Sibling: needle, and the Relic extension of Still Pin. The push is drive taken 48 percent BELOW the Tier 1 floor: at 0.26 the equilibrium lean falls to 0.0152 against needle's 0.0193 and the travel term in spin decay nearly vanishes, so it outlasts the needle in practice while reading lower on the stamina number itself. That is the hidden depth of the part and it is honest physics, not a special case. shaft 0.62 is 21 percent below the floor. Glass is the drawback that fits a top which spends its whole endgame under 40 percent spin: measured on the reference chassis it costs 13.6 points of win rate, turns 258 spinout wins into 122 and lifts knockout losses from 37 to 83. Not better than needle on any axis except its own low drive. Measured ceiling 42.5, pull 36.6 against needle 53.2 and taper 43.6.

notes:
EMPIRICALLY TESTED. I did not edit any repo file. I built a patched scratch copy of sim2.js at /tmp/claude-1000/-workspaces-lucid-winds/20a4fdff-a3a0-46de-8c48-50f49653330c/scratchpad/sim2p.js with all 14 parts and the one new drawback wired, plus a bit only copy of tools/partaudit.js, and iterated the numbers against measured results over four full audit passes and about a dozen focused probes.

FINAL AUDIT RESULT, node bitaudit.js 10 3 44, 24 bits:
  Zero power creep flags. Every one of the 14 new parts is inside +4 mean of its nearest ceiling Tier 1 sibling.
  Weight count spread 9.7 points, passes. Imbalance bands still healthy, feral 45.4 percent and still the best band.
  Ceiling spread 25.0 points, which is EXACTLY the Tier 1 only spread, needle 66.3 to taper 41.3. My 14 parts span 41.3 to 65.0, entirely inside the existing envelope, so this proposal adds nothing to the slot's known ceiling problem. The audit still prints FAILED on that line, but it fails on inherited Tier 1 geometry, not on anything here. Re run at the real budget, node tools/partaudit.js 800 2, before trusting the exact figures; pull carries roughly plus or minus 3 points of noise at my budget and the sibling matching is itself noisy because it keys off ceiling.

ONE NEW DRAWBACK, not two. Add to the DRAWBACKS array:
  { id: 'skittish', name: 'Skittish',
    desc: 'It will slide out of the dish at a speed anything else would ride out.' }
The exact one line of physics, replacing the existing need line in stepTop step 8:
  const need = K.exitNeed * g.exitNeed * (s.dw && s.dw.skittish ? 0.55 : 1) * (sector > 0.62 ? K.pocketMu : 1) * (a.t < a.anchor ? 6 : 1);
Used by two parts, rasp and pintle. Measured cost 2.0 points on rasp and 6.2 on pintle, with ringout losses roughly doubling in both cases, so it fires and it costs points as well as rounds.

A SECOND DRAWBACK I WROTE AND THEN THREW AWAY, because the measurement said it was decoration. It was 'scrub', baseline decay times 1.35, one line folded into the greed term. On pintle it moved the outcome 0.3 points and did not change the finish mix at all. The reason is worth keeping: a defensive top on the reference chassis survives the full 60 second round limit on spin alone, so baseline decay is not what decides its rounds and a decay drawback on a fortress is power creep in a costume. Do not let anyone add it back for another slot without measuring it on that slot's own profile.

THE DRIVE CLIFF, the single most useful thing I found, and it will bite the blade and ratchet streams too. drive is self taxing and the tax is quadratic: the slip term in spin decay is proportional to the drive force, the drive force is proportional to drive times lean, and equilibrium lean is itself proportional to drive. Measured on the attack chassis, 400 rounds each:
  drive 1.88  win 43.0 percent   drive 2.10  win 38.8   drive 2.20  win 26.0   drive 2.35  win 15.8
At 2.35 the top loses 300 of 400 rounds to its OWN spinout. Best of ten chassis ceiling falls from 61.3 at drive 2.10 to 36.3 at 2.35. So a nominal 25 percent push on drive is not a specialisation, it is an unbuildable part, and Spur is deliberately at 2.15 for that reason. If you want the tier arithmetic to read uniformly, the honest framing is that the simulation collects the other 11 percent of the push itself.

THE THREE MIDDLE PROFILE PARTS the brief asked for are sabot, ferrule and cleat. All three keep stamina, drive and dash inside the usable middle and spend their tier budget on stable, shaft and rail grip, which are the axes a mixed build does not have to rebuild around. cleat is the one I care most about: it is a rail dash a stamina or defense chassis can actually buy, which is the direct answer to the note that attack tips only read well inside a coherent attack chassis.

PAY CURRENCIES are deliberately spread so the slot does not read as one trade repeated: stable pays four times, shaft four, drive twice, stamina twice, and Sabot and Ferrule are an exact mirror pair, one buying standing up with fragility and the other buying staying together with falling over.

CONVENTION I USED, state it in CATALOG.md if you want the tiers to read consistently: a Tier 2 push is the Tier 1 extreme times 1.25 or divided by 1.25, and the paid stat goes further past the opposite extreme in the same percentage terms, typically 28 to 41 percent. Tier 3 pushes run 39 to 49 percent. Two stats sit outside the Tier 1 range on every Forged part and no more; a third stat outside the range would be a second push in disguise.

TWO PARTS TO WATCH ON THE FULL AUDIT. rowel and rasp both land pull 27.6 against claw 25.2, so they sit inside the gate by about 2 points and the gate's sibling choice is noisy. stable is the dial on both; an earlier rowel at stable 0.56 read 33.5 and tripped the flag. Going the other way, spur reads pull 12.3, the lowest in the slot; that is not a gate failure, its ceiling of 56.3 proves it is buildable, but if you want it nearer claw the dial is shaft 0.56 to 0.68, worth about 6 points.

CORUNDUM IS INVISIBLE TO THE GATE. Greedy's cost lands entirely on the scoreboard, converting 1 point spinout losses into 2 point knockouts, 62 to 156 in 1200 rounds, while round win rate moves +0.5. partaudit measures rounds, not points, so it will read that drawback as free. Corundum passes on pull anyway at 41.2 against needle's 53.2, but if you ever build a points weighted audit, greedy parts are where it will earn its keep.

Ids are clear of every existing part id in all five slots, of the seven tuning operation ids and of the eighteen ability ids. All names are generic English tool, mineral and workshop words with no franchise or product association. No em dash, en dash or hyphen appears in any name or description.
